subject: Coffee & Tea
title: Coffee Belt Geography
description: A micro-lesson that makes Coffee Belt Geography usable.

hook.text: Coffee only grows between the Tropics of Cancer and Capricorn—a band called the Coffee Belt.

buildup.text: The belt spans 70+ countries, but just five—Brazil, Vietnam, Colombia, Indonesia, Ethiopia—grow most of it.

discovery.text: Altitude matters enormously. The best arabica grows between 1,200 and 2,000 meters above sea level.

twist.text: Climate change is shrinking suitable coffee land. By 2050, half of current growing areas may be too hot.

climax.text: Countries like China and Nepal are emerging as new coffee origins as traditional regions warm up.

punchline.text: The belt that grows your coffee is slowly shifting.

quiz.question: What is the 'Coffee Belt'?
options: The tropical zone between Cancer and Capricorn where coffee grows

details.summary: The coffee belt is the tropical zone between the Tropics of Cancer and Capricorn where conditions allow coffee cultivation. Altitude, soil, rainfall, and temperature within this band determine whether a region can grow arabica, robusta, or both. Over 70 countries sit within the belt.
details.whyItMatters: Geography dictates coffee's fate. The belt concentrates production in developing tropical nations, creating economic dependence and climate vulnerability.
takeaways: The coffee belt spans the tropics between 25 degrees north and south
Altitude and climate within the belt determine which species grow
Over 70 countries produce coffee within this zone

faq.question: What conditions define the coffee belt?
faq.answer: Consistent temperatures between 15 and 25 degrees Celsius, annual rainfall of 1500 to 3000 millimeters, no frost, and well-drained soil. Arabica prefers higher altitudes and cooler temperatures within the belt, while robusta grows at lower elevations with more heat and humidity.

faq.question: Are the borders of the coffee belt shifting?
faq.answer: Climate change is shifting viable growing zones. Lower elevations within the belt are becoming too hot, while higher elevations and areas at the belt's edges may become newly viable. The belt is not so much shrinking as moving, with profound consequences for farming communities.
